alignments.note: Verb inflection supplies the English subject pronoun.

Substantival article before idios supplies the possessive: rule 54 reads ta idia -> *his own* as *his* to the article and *own* to the adjective, as rule 47 reads ek ton idion -> *of his own*. Corrected from unrepresented; BSB reports this article represented and here that report is right.
The adjective keeps its own word; idios cannot say whose, so the possessive is the article's.
A substantival article whose complement is a predicate adjective keeps the antecedent pronoun and the relativizer together under rule 31 (Ho pistos -> *He that*). Corrected from a bare *they*.

The adjective keeps the supplied copula and its own word. *his* stays here rather than with the article because the article is already spent on *they that* (rule 76's availability test); a discontinuous *they that ... his* on the article under rule 15 remains defensible.

review_notes: The two idios clauses divide by configuration, not by lexeme: substantival ta idia gives the article *his* (rules 47, 54), while the attributive ton adelphon ton idion at 1:41 leaves both articles empty (rule 47).
The ASV note (Greek his own things) bears on the gender of the first phrase, not on the article's status.
